newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: Mozambique wins almost $1 billion in foreign finance.
newsitem.headline: Mozambique wins almost $1 billion in foreign finance.

text.p: Mozambican Prime Minister Pascoal Mocumbi said on Saturday he expected foreign financing for the Mozambican economy to reach $955 million this year, $15 million more than the $940 million of 1996.

Speaking to reporters on his return from the annual meeting in Paris of the World Bank's Consultative Group on Mozambique, he said the government's funding requirements put before the group had been fully met.

Confirmed credits and pledged donations amounted to $560 million. Mocumbi said the breakdown of this was 55 percent for investment, 28 percent for balance of payments support, six percent for food aid and 11 percent for "other programmes" such as mine clearance and local elections planned for this year.

The rest of the $955 million was accounted for by debt relief, and by a credit from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which is at an advanced stage of negotiation. Mocumbi was confident there would be no last-minute hitch in granting the credit.
He said the meeting produced "excellent results, particularly when we refer to the quality of the dialogue between Mozambique and its partners".
"The dialogue is no longer about coping with emergencies," he said. "It's about the medium and even the long term."
The Consultative Group had switched away from "urgent, short-term vision" to a consideration of development over the longer term.

Mocumbi said the donors in Paris had agreed with the government's priorities -- including providing small-scale credit for the peasant family sector in agriculture, strengthening the national business class and reforming public administration.
He said that facilitating the growth of the private sector meant providing a friendlier legal environment by reducing unnecessary red tape and also ensuring access to credit.
This meant dealing with debts that businesses had accumulated -- through no fault of their own -- during the civil war which ended in 1992.
One of the government's schemes accepted by the Paris meeting is for a fund which will be used to pay off these companies' debts to the banks, thus making them eligible again for credit.

Among the reforms proposed in public administration was a substantial wage increase in the civil service and a widening of wage differentials to attract and retain qualified staff in the middle and upper levels of the state apparatus.

Mocumbi said no objections had been raised to the scheme. In the past, the IMF has objected to such wage rises on the grounds that they generate inflation. But this time it was going along with the idea.
